name: Bipolaris leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed hemp leaf-spot and blight disease associated with Bipolaris gigantea. Kentucky field studies add useful temporal and canopy context, but lesion appearance overlaps other fungal, bacterial, insect, and abiotic injuries and cannot resolve species, genotype, ploidy, or transmission source.
affectedParts: middle and upper canopy leaves for paired comparison
nearby symptomatic weeds as unproven epidemiological context
indicators: Compatible disease begins as localized necrotic leaf spots and can progress to extensive leaf blight, but no single lesion shape or color is diagnostic.

In two Kentucky experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; capture planting date and repeated observations rather than treating this timing as universal.
Those experiments found greater disease in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, so a useful capture pairs both levels; cultivar, site, and season can alter the pattern.
Photograph the full plant and intact leaf before macro views so lesion burden, canopy level, leaf age, margins, centers, coalescence, and any defoliation remain linked.
Record both leaf surfaces and include a scale and neutral color reference because surface growth, reproductive structures, and color can separate important differentials.
Compatible Bipolaris conidia or culture from the photographed lesion strengthens the label, but recovery alone does not establish causation when other organisms are present.

Lesion-linked ITS and partial 28S evidence supported the original Kentucky report; broader multilocus work documented multiple B. gigantea genotypes and ploidy states that photographs cannot distinguish.
Nearby symptomatic weeds can provide sampling context, but their presence does not prove the infection source or direction of movement.
exclusions: Dark pycnidia embedded in lesions and a Septoria-confirmed isolate support Septoria leaf spot rather than Bipolaris.
Pale-centered round lesions with melanized conidiophores and a Cercospora-confirmed isolate support Cercospora.
Sooty or olivaceous reproductive growth concentrated on the lower surface and appropriate laboratory evidence support Pseudocercospora.
Concentric zonation or central dark sporulation plus a lesion-linked Alternaria identification support Alternaria, although rings alone are nonspecific.
Center cracking or loss must be followed from an intact lesion; physical holes, chewing, hail tears, handling damage, or training injury exclude a symptom-only Bipolaris label.
Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a lesion-linked bacterial isolate support bacterial leaf spot.
A sharp spray, row, field-edge, lighting, irrigation, or contact boundary with no compatible organism supports abiotic or chemical injury.
A different dominant lesion-linked pathogen, mixed recovery without causal resolution, or symptomless inoculated controls excludes a confirmed B. gigantea label.

progression.description: Record matched symptom-free plants, cultivar, planting date, canopy levels, field position, recent weather, irrigation, and exposure history.
Tag intact localized spots and photograph the whole plant, whole leaf, both surfaces, and calibrated lesion macro views before tissue removal.
Reimage tagged leaves and map new lesions to determine whether necrotic area and lesion number increase rather than relying on unrelated single frames.
Document coalescing necrosis, canopy loss, and defoliation while preserving representative advancing margins for laboratory work.
Link each culture, morphology result, molecular result, and any pathogenicity test back to the photographed plant and lesion.

lookAlikes: Caterpillar, beetle, slug, or snail feeding
Hail, wind, handling, or training tear
Nutrient, salinity, drought, or root-zone stress
confirmation: Capture the same intact lesions through progression and preserve plant ID, cultivar, planting date, canopy level, both leaf surfaces, field map, exposure history, and collection time.
Examine advancing lesion margins and both surfaces with magnification for pycnidia, conidiophores, conidia, bacterial signs, arthropods, or physical tearing before selecting a label.
Submit tissue spanning healthy and advancing lesion margins; recover and document a dominant compatible fungus while retaining mixed-organism results rather than selecting the closest visual class.
Use lesion-linked fungal morphology and validated molecular evidence for a Bipolaris organism label; preserve loci, sequence quality, database/version, and isolate identifiers.
Require validated multilocus evidence when exact B. gigantea placement or genotype-level interpretation matters; ITS-only, single-locus, morphology-only, and image-only evidence remain provisional.

When causality matters, require symptom reproduction, recovery of the same organism, and symptomless appropriate controls; nearby weed isolates alone do not establish source or transmission direction.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, ITS-only, single-locus-only, low-resolution, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, and unverified samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve representative untreated tissue and traceable photographs before removing heavily affected material.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness while diagnosis is pending.
Map affected plants against cultivar blocks, canopy levels, irrigation, airflow, field edges, residue, weeds, and possible exposure boundaries.
correctivePlan: Use a disease-management plan appropriate to the organism confirmed by the diagnostic laboratory and the production setting.
Remove or contain confirmed diseased material and residue as locally appropriate, then monitor tagged plants for new lesions.
Evaluate response using new lesion incidence and severity records; old necrotic tissue will not become healthy after correction.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic plants, tools, or debris into clean areas.
Improve air circulation, limit avoidable leaf wetness, and manage infected crop or weed residue where feasible.
Scout consistent plant IDs across canopy levels and over time so early spots, disease increase, and confounders can be separated.
warnings: Necrotic spots, expanding blight, canopy loss, and weed co-occurrence are not individually specific to Bipolaris.

The seven-to-eight-week onset, middle-canopy predominance, cultivar differences, and combined-disease yield results are study-specific observations, not universal Bipolaris timing, distribution, susceptibility, yield, or action thresholds.
The original report used ITS and partial 28S placement, while later multilocus work found multiple genotypes and ploidy states; photographs cannot resolve this diversity.
Recovery from a lesion or nearby weed does not by itself prove causation, infection source, or transmission direction.
No image or video was indexed because no stable, item-level, plant-linked B. gigantea asset with sufficiently clear reuse and training rights was verified.
All symptom-only, detached, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, single-locus-only, low-resolution, and rights-unclear samples require human review.

sources.title: First Report of Hemp Leaf Spot Caused by a Bipolaris Species on Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Outdoor hemp in Kentucky developed severe necrotic leaf spot and blight associated with a lineage identified morphologically as Drechslera gigantea and placed within Bipolaris by ITS and partial 28S sequence analysis.
Inoculated hemp leaves developed symptoms while noninoculated controls remained symptomless, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.
The fungus was also associated with symptomatic dicot and monocot weeds in affected fields, but co-occurrence does not establish the direction or source of transmission.

This regional first report supports a Cannabis-specific Bipolaris disease; it does not establish universal lesion morphology, canopy preference, timing, prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, yield loss, or action thresholds.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

sources.title: Seeing double on Cannabis: Haploids and heteroploids of Bipolaris gigantea on hemp and other dicots
sources.publisher: Taylor & Francis on behalf of the Mycological Society of America
supportedClaims: The study examined Bipolaris gigantea isolates from hemp leaf-spot lesions and nearby weeds collected across 11 Kentucky counties.
Twenty-three isolates were analyzed by multilocus phylogenetics and seven were also whole-genome sequenced, revealing multiple genotypes and both haploid and apparently heteroploid isolates.
Haploid and heteroploid isolates caused similar disease on hemp, so lesion appearance cannot resolve ploidy, genotype, or the source host.

Species- and genotype-level labels therefore require lesion-linked laboratory evidence; a symptom photograph or single recovered isolate cannot establish population structure or transmission direction.
